newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-TRAGEDY AT GRAND NATIONAL FOR JENNY PITMAN.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-TRAGEDY AT GRAND NATIONAL FOR JENNY PITMAN.

text.p: For trainer Jenny Pitman, the 1997 Grand National offered the ultimate tragedy.

In floods of tears when the race was abandoned on Saturday after a suspected Irish Republican Army (IRA) bomb alert, she was among the most vociferous supporters of the race being rescheduled on Monday.
Then Pitman, a trainer who wears her heart on her sleeve and worries constantly about the well-being of her charges, had to face the agony of her fancied runner, Smith's Band, breaking his neck.
The hotly-fancied steeplechaser was contesting the lead with the eventual winner Lord Gyllene when he crashed at the 20th fence and died instantly.

His grieving rider, dual Grand National winning jockey Richard Dunwoody, said: "He was hanging and jumping a bit right all the way. I was quite happy with the pace. We weren't going mad and I had Suny Bay and Lord Gyllene up with me.
"The horse never took off when he fell. It is very sad. He didn't deserve a fate like that."
The Grand National has shown how kind and how cruel it can be to the Pitman family over the years.

Richard Pitman, Jenny's former husband, rode the mighty Australian Crisp in a wonderful display of front-running in 1973 which ended sadly for him with Red Rum just running out the narrow winner on the unforgiving long run-in.
Jenny Pitman's son Mark also had victory dashed from his lips in 1991 when the valiant Garrison Savannah was just beaten by Seagram.

Jenny Pitman became the first woman ever to train a Grand National winner when her beloved Corbiere landed the world's most famous steeplechase in 1983. She repeated the feat in 1995 with Royal Athlete.
But the Grand National dealt her a cruel blow in 1993 when her Esha Ness won "the race that never was".
Few racegoers will ever forget the look of agonised astonishment on the face of jockey Jimmy White when he realised he had won a race that was eventually declared void after two false starts.
Mark Pitman said his heart really bled for his mother after Smith's Band's tragic accident.
"You try as a trainer to minimise the risks but it is like everything else in every walk of life. There are risks attached to racing," he said.
"I don't think you can blame the race as fatalities happen unfortunately on all racecourses," he said.
